prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Spotify Technology S.A." (ticker SPOT), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SPOT", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Spotify Technology S.A.

mission.statement: Our mission is to deliver creativity to the world—one note, one voice, one idea at a time.
mission.source: Spotify newsroom company information page (newsroom.spotify.com/company-info), checked October 2026
mission.plain: Spotify wants to bring music, talk and stories from creators to everyone on Earth.

about.plain: Spotify is an app that lets you listen to almost any song, podcast or audiobook on your phone, computer, car or TV. You can listen for free if you hear some ads, or pay a monthly fee for no ads and extra features. It learns what you like and makes playlists just for you. It pays music companies and creators for the songs and shows people play.
about.customers: Hundreds of millions of everyday listeners (777 million monthly users, 300 million paying, in mid-2026) plus advertisers who pay to reach them.
about.everyday: It is the green app many people use to play music on the bus, at the gym or through a smart speaker at home.

money.plain: monthly plans with no ads, offline listening and audiobook hours
ads played or shown to free listeners and in podcasts
audiobook listening hours in Premium plus add-on hours and single-book purchases
video shows that earn ad money shared with creators
AI tools that build music to order, which could support pricier tiers

result.summary: Spotify has a real but not impregnable advantage: it is the world's largest music subscription service (31.4% of global music subscribers at end-2025 per MIDiA), with the biggest user base, the best-regarded personalisation and years of each user's listening history and playlists. Its main weakness is that it licenses the same catalogue as Apple, Amazon and YouTube, and the record labels take most of each subscription euro, so gross margin is only about 32-33%.

pricingPower.evidence: Spotify raised the US Individual Premium price to $10.99 in July 2023, $11.99 in July 2024 and $12.99 in February 2026 (Duo to $18.99, Family to $21.99), yet Premium subscribers kept growing from 263M at end-2024 to 290M at end-2025 and 300M in Q2 2026, and the company cites price increases as a driver of Premium ARPU growth; gross margin is still only about 33% because labels capture most of the revenue.

moats.evidence: Spotify is the default name for music streaming in most Western markets, with 777M monthly users in 184 markets, and its annual Wrapped campaign is a global cultural event.

Years of saved playlists, liked songs, follows and a personalised algorithm trained on each user's history make moving to Apple Music or YouTube Music inconvenient, though the catalogue itself is the same elsewhere.

More listeners give more data for recommendations and make Spotify the first stop for artists and podcasters (7 million podcast titles), and shared playlists and Wrapped spread socially, but music itself is not exclusive.

Scale lets Spotify spread R&D and marketing over €17.2B of 2025 revenue, lifting operating margin from -3.4% in 2023 to 12.8% in 2025, but royalties (most of its €11.7B cost of revenue) scale with revenue.
Global music streaming supports several large rivals (Apple, Amazon, YouTube, Tencent Music), so the market is not a natural monopoly.
Spotify's free ad-supported tier as a funnel to paid plans was hard for Apple to copy, but Amazon and YouTube now run similar free-plus-paid models.
Spotify's long record of personalisation (Discover Weekly, DJ, Prompted Playlist) and of shipping over 50 major platform improvements in 2025 reflects strong product know-how.
Music catalogues are licensed non-exclusively from the major labels; only some podcasts (e.g., The Joe Rogan Experience deal) and its first-party listening data are distinctive.

customers.evidence: Premium subscribers kept growing through three US price rises (263M end-2024, 290M end-2025, 300M in Q2 2026) and MAUs reached 777M; Spotify had the most net subscriber additions of any service in 2025 per MIDiA.

talent.evidence: Glassdoor shows a 3.9/5 rating with 79% of employees recommending it; Spotify is seen as an attractive tech employer in Europe, but it cut about 17% of staff in December 2023 and had 7,323 employees at end-2025.

product.evidence: Spotify is widely regarded as having the best personalisation and cross-device experience (Spotify Connect in cars, speakers, TVs and consoles), and it combines music, podcasts, video podcasts and audiobooks in one app; Apple Music beats it on lossless/spatial history, though Spotify added lossless in 2025.

competitors.name: Apple (Apple Music)
competitors.note: Apple Music held 12.6% of global music subscribers at end-2025 (MIDiA) and is pre-installed and bundled on iPhones; Apple also controls App Store rules Spotify depends on.

competitors.name: Alphabet (YouTube Music / YouTube Premium)
competitors.note: Fastest-growing music service two years running, with 12.4% of global subscribers at end-2025, bundled in YouTube Premium; YouTube is also the largest podcast platform.

competitors.name: Amazon (Amazon Music, Audible)
competitors.note: Amazon Music (8.5% of global subscribers) is bundled with Prime and Alexa; Audible is the leading audiobook rival.

competitors.name: Tencent Music Entertainment (QQ Music, Kugou, Kuwo)
competitors.note: China's dominant music platform with 13.8% of global subscribers; Spotify does not operate in mainland China, so overlap is mainly for label deals and global scale.

competitors.name: ByteDance (TikTok)
competitors.note: Short-video app where much music discovery now happens; competes for listening time and young users.

competitors.name: SiriusXM (Pandora, SiriusXM Podcast Network)
competitors.note: US satellite radio, Pandora streaming and podcast ads compete for in-car and home listening and audio ad budgets.

competitors.name: Deezer
competitors.note: French music streamer competing mainly in France and partner bundles.

competitors.name: Netflix (video podcasts)
competitors.note: Entered video podcasts, where Spotify is building its creator programme; competes for screen time and shows.

competitors.name: iHeartMedia
competitors.note: Large US podcast publisher and radio broadcaster competing for podcast audiences and audio ad dollars.

competitors.name: Block (Tidal)
competitors.note: Tidal is a smaller hi-fi, artist-focused music service.

competitors.name: NetEase Cloud Music
competitors.note: China's second-largest music platform; no direct overlap as Spotify is absent from China.

competitors.name: SoundCloud
competitors.note: Private service popular with independent and emerging artists.

competitors.name: Anghami
competitors.note: Music streaming leader in the Middle East and North Africa, where Spotify also competes.

competitors.name: JioSaavn (Reliance)
competitors.note: Leading Indian music streamer, owned by Reliance group, competing in a large low-priced market.

marketShare.market: Global music streaming subscribers (MIDiA Research; end-2025 vs end-2020)

threats: YouTube Music is gaining global share fastest (7.9% of subscribers in 2020 to 12.4% at end-2025) and is bundled with YouTube Premium.
Record labels control the catalogue and take most revenue; tougher licensing terms or 'artist-centric' royalty demands could cap gross margin.
Apple, Amazon and Google can bundle music with devices, Prime or YouTube at little marginal cost, and Apple controls iOS app-store rules.
AI-generated music and AI assistants could change how people discover and listen to music, weakening playlists as a gatekeeper.
Royalty disputes such as the Mechanical Licensing Collective lawsuit over Spotify's audiobook bundle (amended complaint filed October 2025).
Reputational backlash, such as artist boycotts in 2025 over founder Daniel Ek's investment firm leading a funding round for defence-AI company Helsing.
Leadership transition to a co-CEO structure from January 2026 after founder Daniel Ek stepped up to Executive Chairman.
A strong euro has cut reported growth (Q1 2026 revenue +8% reported vs +14% at constant currency).

ceo.name: Alex Norström and Gustav Söderström (co-CEOs); founder Daniel Ek is Executive Chairman
ceo.background: Long-time Spotify executives: Söderström, an engineer and former mobile-startup founder, ran product and technology; Norström, a business-school-trained executive, ran the subscription and content business; both joined in 2009-2011.

c1.evidence: Spotify leads global music streaming with 31.4% of the 921.6 million music subscribers at end-2025 (MIDiA), a market that grew 10.1% in 2025 and is still expanding in emerging markets.

c2.evidence: Listeners choose Spotify for its personalisation, free tier and app on every device, which kept subscribers growing through three US price rises, but rivals license the same music, so the edge rests on product and habit rather than exclusive content.

c3.evidence: Spotify is a household name with 777 million monthly users in 184 markets and is the default music app for many people, much as Netflix is for TV.

c4.evidence: Spotify has long stated a creator-centred mission (now 'to deliver creativity to the world—one note, one voice, one idea at a time') and record payouts to the music industry, but the 2025 Helsing controversy and heavy founder share sales temper the purpose story.

c6.evidence: “music, playlists, Wrapped, underpays artists” — the public impression is mostly positive among listeners, who love the product and Wrapped, but many artists criticise low per-stream payouts and the 2025 boycott over Ek's Helsing investment.

c7.evidence: Spotify rides the secular shift from radio, CDs and downloads to streaming audio, with music subscribers worldwide rising from 472.2 million in 2020 to 921.6 million in 2025 (MIDiA) and podcasts and audiobooks adding new markets.

c8.evidence: It has already expanded from music into podcasts (7 million titles), video podcasts and audiobooks (700,000 titles), and is testing AI-driven features such as Prompted Playlist that could support higher-priced tiers.

m1.evidence: Founder Daniel Ek, now Executive Chairman setting capital allocation and long-term strategy, has a clear vision of an audio platform for creators; the new co-CEOs frame AI as a way to give listeners more control.

m2.evidence: The co-CEOs are not founders but have spent more than 15 years building Spotify, and founder Daniel Ek remains Executive Chairman with major voting power.

m4.evidence: The co-CEOs' January 2026 letter stresses products that leave people 'feeling better after each session' and record payouts to artists, but there is little independent evidence of servant leadership.

m5.evidence: Spotify's culture of small autonomous squads became a widely copied engineering model and keeps shipping features like DJ, Prompted Playlist, SongDNA and video podcasts.

m6.evidence: Co-CEO Gustav Söderström led product and technology for years and is deeply hands-on with product; co-CEO Alex Norström comes from the business side.

m7.evidence: No major scandals involve the co-CEOs; Spotify pays out the large majority of revenue to rights holders, but criticism of artist pay and Ek's defence investment shows mixed views of the company's character.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech at a top university by co-CEOs Alex Norström or Gustav Söderström (or founder Daniel Ek) was found.

m8b.evidence: The co-CEOs are relatively low-profile executives; founder Daniel Ek is well known in tech but not a celebrity personality on the scale of Musk.

m9.evidence: Under the team that now runs it, operating income went from a €446M loss in 2023 to €1,365M in 2024 and €2,198M in 2025, and Q2 2026 operating income of €655M beat the €630M guidance.

m10.evidence: Spotify cut about 17% of staff in December 2023 and research and development spending fell from €1,725M in 2023 to €1,393M in 2025, a turn to frugality after years of heavy spending.

c10.evidence: Spotify gives 777 million people in 184 markets access to almost all recorded music, millions of podcasts and audiobooks, much of it free with ads.

p2.evidence: Running a reliable personalised streaming service for hundreds of millions of users and building recommendation AI is hard, but the music itself is licensed and rivals offer similar services.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 25.6% in 2020 to 32.0% in 2025 and operating margin from -3.7% to 12.8%, though both dipped in 2022.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Spotify had €9,388M of cash and short-term investments, no exchangeable notes after repaying them in Q1 2026, and €8,385M of shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from -€293M in 2020 to €2,198M in 2025 and operating cash flow from €259M to €2,933M, though 2022 and 2023 were weak years.

v1.evidence: Many listeners see Spotify as the best music app because its recommendations and playlists are better and it works on every device, but Apple Music, YouTube Music and Amazon Music offer nearly the same catalogue at similar prices.

v2.evidence: Spotify has a 3.9/5 Glassdoor rating with 79% recommending it and has won employer-brand awards (e.g., LinkedIn Best Employer Brand Nordics 2019), but it does not feature in top global best-places-to-work rankings.

c5.evidence: If Spotify disappeared, hundreds of millions of listeners would lose their playlists and free access to music, and artists and podcasters would lose a major source of income and discovery, though rivals would fill much of the gap.
